A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same FlashTrace research. The main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison. v2 retains Appendices A–I and adds Appendices J–N.

before.justification: v1 reports original attribution-quality, runtime, memory, ablation and generalization results on RULER, MATH, MoreHopQA and Aider, including appendix analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds HotpotQA evaluations without correctness filtering, attention-caching measurements and last-token targeting results in Tables 8–10.

M1.justification: The proximity-based span aggregation, recursive reweighting and final accumulation in Section 4 and Algorithm 1 are unchanged. On-the-fly attention recomputation was already mentioned in v1 Appendix B.2; v2 explains and benchmarks that option. Last-token targeting is an ablation, not a replacement method.

E1.justification: The benchmark and task suite is retained. Appendix K broadens HotpotQA evaluation beyond correctly answered generations by removing correctness filtering, and evaluates longer input contexts. This extends the tested population and conditions within an existing task.

E2.justification: Table 10 adds a Last-Token comparator against FlashTrace on HotpotQA. Existing comparisons remain intact, and Table 8 uses the existing IFR and AttnLRP baselines. The newly cited feature-circuit methods are discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Original experimental settings are retained. Appendix K adds unfiltered HotpotQA tests at 2048 and 4096 tokens, beyond the filtered 1024-token setting. Appendix L adds a cached-versus-recomputed attention benchmark using Qwen-3 4B in bf16 at 2048 tokens; Appendix M adds a target-scope control. These are additional protocols, not revisions to the existing tables.

E4.justification: Appendices K–M substantially extend validation of key design choices: robustness to correctness filtering and longer contexts, the memory–runtime trade-off of attention caching, and last-token versus full-span attribution. These address questions not tested by v1's existing recursion-depth, exhaustive-rollout and generalization analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix L and Table 9 newly report five-run latency averages with ± values for both caching modes. The meaning of the ± values is unspecified. This adds repeated-measurement reporting for a new experiment, without establishing increased runs or new statistical testing for the retained results.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results are retained, while Tables 8–10 add substantive robustness, resource and ablation findings. Unfiltered HotpotQA yields FlashTrace RISE/MAS of 0.036/0.118 at 2048 tokens and 0.025/0.106 at 4096 tokens. Recomputation reduces memory from 35.43 to 13.43 GiB while increasing latency from 1.98 to 2.81 seconds. Table 10 adds Last-Token coverage of 0.161 versus the repeated FlashTrace value of 0.384. These are additional comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, aggregation and recursion equations, normalization approximation and complexity derivations are retained. Appendix A.1 adds prose reasoning about the inherited normalization treatment and error accumulation, but no new formal assumption, error bound, derivation or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: efficient and faithful multi-token attribution through span aggregation and recursion, over 130× speedup, and generalization across tasks and models. Additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 newly distinguishes informational contribution from direct causal effect, and Appendix A.1 adds an argument about normalization-error accumulation. Appendices M–N introduce semantic cancellation, diffuse evidence and spurious structural-token salience as limitations, advising coarse localization rather than precise token-level interpretation in difficult cases. These substantially expand the previously limited discussion of applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: The abstract newly supplies a FlashTrace code repository address. Appendix L explains layer-wise attention recomputation and discarding, and specifies the bf16 configuration for its new resource benchmark. Original algorithm, hardware and dataset-construction documentation is retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix J add Dunefsky et al.'s transcoders and Hanna et al.'s circuit-tracer, positioning token attribution as complementary to feature-circuit analysis. Appendix A.1 also explicitly attributes the normalization treatment to ALTI and IFR. The broader research positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing wording and section order are preserved. v2 adds Appendices J–N and localized explanatory paragraphs, a conflict-of-interest disclosure, acknowledgements and publication/correspondence information. Equal-contribution markers are removed. These are limited structural and editorial additions.

P2.justification: v2 adds three compact tables, extends the appendix contents listing and adjusts front matter and page flow. Existing tables move with the text, while Figures 1–7 and the organization of existing result displays are retained. There is no broad visual redesign.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the evidence beyond v1's filtered, 1024-token HotpotQA evaluation and adds useful memory and target-scope comparisons in Tables 8–10. The code pointer and explicit failure conditions also improve reproducibility information and interpretation. The gain is limited: the new HotpotQA study changes filtering and context length together without reporting sample sizes or uncertainty, and the prediction that sentence-level results should be at least as strong is not experimentally demonstrated.
